analysis.title: Inside The Jobs Rollercoaster: How August's Seasonal "Gift" Came Due In September, And Squeezed The Bond Shorts
key_insights: September payrolls rose 29K versus a 90K consensus and below all ~80 estimates, including Barclays' Street-low 50K. Unemployment rounded up to 4.2% and average hourly earnings rose 0.1%.
August was revised down from 162K to 133K and July to -10K, which leaves July and August combined 60K lower than previously reported.

Raw (not seasonally adjusted) payrolls rose 333K in September, above the 317K raw gain in September 2025. Seasonal adjustment removed 304K this year versus 198K last year, so the headline fell to 29K from 119K.
The 304K September seasonal haircut is the largest since 2021 and close to the 2015-25 average of -305K. After several gentle years, the seasonal factors reverted to their historical norm.
August's 162K headline came from a positive +8K seasonal adjustment, only the second positive one in a decade, while raw hiring (+154K) was below the prior year's +200K.

Barclays estimated that August with 2025's seasonal factors would have shown a 74K job loss. The author's rough version of the same exercise puts September at about +135K, above Nomura's 130K high forecast.

BofA's explanation is the survey calendar. The payroll survey week is the one containing the 12th, and this year July to August was four weeks instead of five, so the usual August subtraction was too large and nearly vanished. BofA warned of September payback and forecast +60K.
The author's check since 2015 supports the calendar story. In five-week years the August seasonal subtraction averaged 162K, versus 61K in four-week years (excluding 2020 and this year).

Labor Day fell on September 7, the latest possible date. Goldman noted that Septembers with a late Labor Day saw payroll growth at or below trend. 2026 has the same calendar as 2015, when the September seasonal adjustment took away 416K jobs.

Combined August and September first-print seasonal drag is -296K, the second lightest of the past decade. On revised data the two-month drag is about -367K, near 2025's -376K, so the author reads the two months as a wash.

Goldman puts the three-month payroll average at 51K and the underlying pace of job growth (payroll plus household surveys) at 51K, roughly its estimate of breakeven. Apollo's Torsten Slok argues breakeven has collapsed from 200,000 a month to close to zero because of lower immigration and retiring baby boomers.

The household survey was strong. The labor force rose 485K and household employment rose 406K, the second-largest gain since January 2025, so the unemployment rate rose only 0.03pp to 4.18% for a benign reason.

Softer details: the payroll diffusion index fell 8.6pt to 49.0, its lowest since October 2025, and downward revisions were concentrated in leisure and hospitality (-92K across two months), a sector Goldman said is hard to seasonally adjust.
The Fed under Warsh delivered its first hike since July 2023 two weeks after the 162K August print. The author argues that print was mostly seasonal adjustment and that July was negative.

Markets removed the October hike. October odds, which topped 75% about a week earlier, were effectively eliminated, and Fed-dated swaps no longer priced a full hike for the rest of 2026 (about 22.5bp remained). Jefferies' Tom Simons called the print the nail in the coffin for an October move.

The bond squeeze worked briefly. Goldman had flagged CTAs as extremely short global bonds (~$390bn notional), with US 10Ys at 99% of max short and 30Ys at 100%. The 10Y yield fell from 5.22% to 5.16%, a new weekly low, and Nvidia hit its first record since May.

The move faded. By 10:20am ET two- and five-year yields were back to pre-payrolls levels after investors digested the strong household survey. Goldman's Rich Privorotsky had warned the back end of the bond market still doesn't care.
The author's takeaway is that neither print is reliable. August's 162K and September's 29K are both distorted, the combined average is about 80K, and BLS will revise both again next month.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Below every one of the ~80 Street estimates and the weakest headline since July, but the author attributes most of the miss to a large seasonal adjustment.
The August blockbuster was inflated by seasonal adjustment and has been cut by 29K.
July is now negative. July and August combined are 60K lower than first reported.
The rise came from a 485K jump in the labor force, not from job losses, with household employment up 406K.
Soft wage growth adds to the case against further Fed hikes.
Underlying raw hiring was stronger than a year ago, so the headline weakness is a seasonal adjustment effect.
Goldman calls this and its 51K underlying growth estimate roughly the breakeven pace.
A new weekly low on the print, but two- and five-year yields were back to pre-payrolls levels by 10:20am ET.

macro_indicators.reading: Above 75% a week earlier, effectively eliminated after the print
macro_indicators.interpretation: Swaps priced about 22.5bp of tightening for the rest of 2026, less than one full hike.

macro_indicators.indicator: Survey interval, July to August payroll weeks
macro_indicators.reading: 4 weeks in 2026 vs 5 weeks in 2024 and 2025
macro_indicators.interpretation: The shorter interval made the standard August seasonal subtraction too large for the period, which then reversed into September.

risk_factors: BLS will revise both August and September again next month, so current headline figures remain unreliable.
Seasonal factors could be more or less punitive than economists penciled in, as BofA warned before the report.
The strong household survey undercuts a labor-collapse narrative and limits how far bond yields can fall.
Policy risk if the Fed tunes rates around the rounding on a single payrolls print, as Goldman's Brian Bingham warned.
Residual seasonality in youth participation and in leisure and hospitality employment may keep distorting the data.
charts_described: Chart of SA minus NSA job change in the first print of each year (BLS Table B-1) shows September 2026 at -304K, near the 2015-25 average of -305K.

Wolfe Research chart (NSA minus SA, sign flipped vs the author's charts) shows August seasonal factors pushed the adjusted print below raw in nearly every year since 2000, often by 150K-200K, and above raw only for the third time this year.
vol_and_positioning: Goldman's Brian Garrett flagged CTAs as extremely short global bonds (~$390bn notional), with US 10Ys at 99% of max short and 30Ys at 100%.
The weak print produced a short squeeze in Treasuries (10Y 5.22% to 5.16%) that faded within hours as two- and five-year yields returned to pre-payrolls levels.
Goldman trader Rich Privorotsky had warned the bond market's back end still doesn't care. The author notes stretched positioning rarely unwinds in a single session.
Small caps and long-duration tech led equities higher on the print, the dollar slipped and gold rose.

tension_points.bull_case: A near-record CTA short (~$390bn notional, 10Ys at 99% of max short) plus a sub-consensus print and an August seasonal payback set up a squeeze. The 10Y fell from 5.22% to 5.16% on the print.
tension_points.bear_case: The strong household survey (employment +406K) sent two- and five-year yields back to pre-payrolls levels by 10:20am ET. Goldman's Privorotsky said the back end still doesn't care, and stretched positioning rarely unwinds in one session.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Two- and five-year yields holding at pre-payrolls levels, as they did by 10:20am ET on the day, shows the squeeze has faded.

tension_points.bull_case: Raw hiring in September exceeded last year, household employment rose 406K and the unemployment rise reflects labor force growth. The author reads August and September together as a wash.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman puts underlying job growth at 51K, about breakeven. The diffusion index fell to 49.0 and leisure and hospitality revisions were -92K.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Next month's BLS revisions to August and September, which the author says will change both figures again.

theme_stances.key_argument: The August strength and September weakness are mostly seasonal adjustment and survey calendar effects, so the two months together show a labor market near breakeven.
theme_stances.evidence: August was never as strong as it looked

theme_stances.key_argument: The CTA short in bonds set up a squeeze on the weak print, but the strong household survey limited its duration.
theme_stances.evidence: Positioning that stretched rarely unwinds in a single session
